report:
**Conclusion:** Your answer is essentially **no for most people**: regular vitamin C does not meaningfully prevent *getting* common colds in the general population.

The strongest evidence is a Cochrane review of 29 randomized trial comparisons (11,306 participants). In ordinary community settings, regular supplementation did not reduce cold incidence; the pooled estimate excluding unusually stressed groups was RR 0.97 (95% CI 0.94–1.00)—at most a very small effect. This is why the review concludes routine supplementation is not justified for prevention.

There is an important exception supporting a qualified “yes”: five trials among marathon runners, skiers, and soldiers on subarctic exercises (598 people) found about a halving of cold risk (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.35–0.64). That evidence may not apply to typical daily life.

Vitamin C may still modestly **shorten** a cold once people taking it regularly become ill (the Cochrane review found consistent duration reductions), but starting it only after symptoms begin has not shown a consistent benefit. Thus, it is not a reliable general cold-prevention strategy, though it could be considered for brief periods of extreme physical stress. Avoid assuming more is better: NIH lists an adult upper intake level of 2,000 mg/day.

Sources:  
- https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold  
- https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/  
- https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8078152/  
- https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminC-HealthProfessional/
